info.title: Re0Auth
info.description: OAuth 2.0 authorization server plus the music-data gateway it fronts. Two error shapes coexist: the OAuth protocol lanes answer the RFC 6749 flat form, everything else answers RFC 9457 problem details whose stable identifier is code.

get.summary: Liveness: the process answers at all. It touches nothing.
Readiness: storage answers, so an orchestrator can route traffic here.

post.summary: Creates a binding flow and returns where to send the browser.
post.description:
Answers JSON rather than a redirect so the caller can keep the CSRF header:
a top-level navigation cannot carry it, and a cross-origin follow is opaque
to a script. The SPA reads the URL and navigates itself.

CSRF-checked like every other state-changing route: without it an attacker
could make a victim's browser start a binding flow the victim never asked
for, and the callback would then attach whatever account the attacker chose.

get.description:
Read-only, so no CSRF: the portal needs this to render a connect action at
all, because a `ConnectorRegistry` resolves by id and cannot enumerate.

200.description: Upstreams the deployment lets the caller bind.

get.description:
No CSRF check here, and that is deliberate: the request is a top-level
browser navigation from the upstream, which cannot carry our header. What
authenticates it is the one-shot state, which only the flow that started it
could produce — and the user comes from that flow, never from this request.

302.description: The binding is stored; the browser returns to the account page.

post.summary:
OIDC Core §5.3.1: the UserInfo Endpoint MUST accept GET and POST. On POST
the token may arrive as a form parameter (RFC 6750 §2.2), but not in
addition to an Authorization header (RFC 6750 §2).

post.description:
Answers `200` with an empty body whenever the request is well-formed, even if
the token is unknown or already revoked. Anything else would let a caller use
this endpoint as an oracle for whether a token exists. A malformed request
(missing `token`, bad `client_id`) still gets an error, because that is a
client bug rather than a probe.

200.description: Always 200 for a well-formed request, even when the token was unknown: answering otherwise would make this endpoint an existence oracle.

BeginBody.description:
The body of a binding start request.

A POST rather than a GET with a query string: starting a flow writes a
pending binding, so a link that any page can trigger is exactly the CSRF
this route used to be unable to defend while it answered 302.

BeginView.description: Where the SPA should send the browser once the flow exists.

BindableUpstreamsView.description: The upstreams a user may start a flow for, as configured.

BindingRevocationSummary.description:
The outcome of the binding killswitch.

A summary rather than a bare count so that adding an upstream revocation
step later does not change the wire contract — but it carries no `failed`
list today, because the local store commits in one transaction and cannot
produce a partial success.

failed.description:
Bindings the cascade left alone because the upstream would not confirm.

A cascade keeps the credential when the upstream cannot be reached
(F-6): the credential is the only way to retry, and deleting it would
hide a token that is still alive upstream. The list makes that visible
instead of reporting a clean sweep.

BindingView.description:
One upstream binding, as shown in the account portal.

Deliberately excludes the sealed sub-credential: the portal needs to know
that a binding exists and whether it is usable, never what it can decrypt to.

last_error_code.description:
The upstream's own error code, e.g. `upstream_401`. Present only when the
binding needs the user to re-authorize.

CreatedClientView.description: The client and its freshly minted secret. The secret appears once.

DiscoveryDocument.description:
The OIDC discovery document.

A struct rather than a `json!` literal: the OpenAPI schema has to come from
the type that serialises the response, and a hand-built object has no type
to derive one from.

Envelope.description: The B8 envelope (ADR-0049). Six fields, no more.

FailedRevocation.description: One binding a cascade could not revoke upstream.

IdentityView.description: One login method as the account page sees it.

issuer.description: The IdP issuer. Shown instead of the subject, which never leaves the server.

IntrospectionResponse.description: RFC 7662 introspection response. Inactive tokens expose only `active`.

JwksDocument.description:
The JWK set, as the signer produced it.

The key entries are passed through verbatim: their fields belong to RFC 7517, and
re-deriving them here would be a second copy of that contract. The document
is parsed into this type rather than forwarded blind, so the response cannot
drift away from the shape the OpenAPI document promises.

KillswitchBody.description:
Admin killswitch: revokes every binding of one user, or the whole instance.

Same per-item cascade as the user-facing killswitch (F-6/B16): an upstream
that refuses keeps its row and shows up in "failed" instead of silently
disappearing from the local database.

MeView.description:
The `/api/me` response body.

A struct rather than a `json!` literal: the SPA mirrors this shape in
`web/src/lib/api.ts`, and `api_contract` compares the two by serialising this
type. A hand-built object cannot be compared to anything, so the drift it
allowed was invisible.

MissingBindingShape.description:
A schema twin of `re0auth_api::ports::MissingBinding`.

The port type lives in the published `re0auth-api` crate, which must not
depend on utoipa, so the schema needs a local copy. The unit test below pins
the two to the same serialised shape.

missing_bindings.description:
What the requested scopes need that the user has not connected yet.

Advisory. The consent screen uses it to offer the missing step; the data
plane re-checks the binding on every read regardless.

ProblemBody.description:
RFC 9457 problem details, for the lanes that are not the OAuth protocol.

Two shapes coexist because the standards disagree: RFC 6749 §5.2 fixes
`error` / `error_description` for the token endpoint, while the gateway and
session lanes have no such constraint and can use the general format. Which one
applies is decided by the lane, not by the error code — the `token` and
`device_authorization` handlers answer RFC 6749 even for errors the gateway
shares a spelling with.

`type` is `about:blank`, which the spec allows when the problem is not further
specified. It is the honest value: we host no problem-type registry, so a URI
under our own domain would not resolve and would be a promise we cannot keep.
The identifier a client can actually branch on is `code`, which is the same
string the error tables are keyed on. For `about:blank` the spec points clients
at the HTTP status, so `title` is the canonical reason phrase and `detail`
carries our explanation.
The RFC 9457 body, named so the schema derives from the type that
serialises the response rather than from a hand-written copy.
